Part II: Static Macroeconomic Models and Comparative Statics

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Connects to: Principles Parts I–II

The models of Principles Part II were presented qualitatively and graphically. The IS curve was a downward-sloping line; the LM curve an upward-sloping one; their intersection determined equilibrium — and shifts of those curves were analyzed by moving pictures in the (Y,i)(Y, i)(Y,i) plane. That graphical approach builds invaluable intuition, but it has limits. It cannot tell you the exact size of the fiscal multiplier as a function of the model parameters. It cannot handle the open-economy extension (Mundell–Fleming) with three markets simultaneously without becoming unwieldy. And it provides no leverage for comparative statics — the precise derivative of equilibrium output with respect to, say, the money supply.

This part strips away the geometry and replaces it with algebra. Every model from Principles Parts I–II is translated into a system of equations, solved explicitly using the linear algebra tools of Chapter 2, and subjected to systematic comparative statics. The payoffs are:

  • Exact multiplier formulas. Not “the output rises” but ΔY∗=h/(h+brk)⋅ΔG\Delta Y^* = h/(h + b_r k)\cdot\Delta GΔY∗=h/(h+br​k)⋅ΔG, from which we can immediately read off when fiscal policy is powerful (large hhh, small brkb_r kbr​k) and when it is impotent (small hhh, or brk→∞b_r k \to \inftybr​k→∞).

  • Policy counterfactuals. Given a specific calibration (say, the U.S. economy in 2009), we can compute exactly what the model predicts about the ARRA multiplier, not merely what direction it points.

  • Transition to dynamic models. The static multipliers derived here are the limiting cases of the dynamic impulse responses we will compute in Parts V–VII. Seeing the connection makes both clearer.

The four chapters cover: the IS–LM model (Chapter 6), the Keynesian cross and multiplier algebra (Chapter 7), the AS–AD model (Chapter 8), and the full taxonomy of fiscal multipliers including the ELB formula (Chapter 9).

Chapter 6: Solving the IS–LM Model¶

Matrix Inversion and Cramer’s Rule for Policy Analysis

“The IS–LM model is simple enough to solve in closed form and rich enough to generate most of the qualitative results of more sophisticated models.”

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 9 (IS–LM derivation and policy analysis); Ch. 22 (fiscal policy); Ch. 23 (monetary policy); Ch. 21 (open economy, Mundell–Fleming) [P:Ch.9, P:Ch.22, P:Ch.23, P:Ch.21]

6.1 From Curves to Equations¶

Principles Chapter 9 derived the IS and LM curves graphically and used them to analyze fiscal and monetary policy. Here we write those curves as explicit linear equations, stack them into a matrix system, and use the tools of Chapter 2 to solve for equilibrium and compute all policy multipliers in closed form.

The strategy has three steps. First, write the IS and LM conditions as two equations in two unknowns (Y,i)(Y, i)(Y,i). Second, solve the 2×22\times22×2 system by matrix inversion or Cramer’s rule. Third, differentiate the solution with respect to every policy variable to obtain the multipliers. Steps one and two require the algebra of Chapter 2; step three uses the implicit function theorem of Chapter 1.

6.1.1 The IS Equation¶

The IS curve is the goods-market equilibrium condition. In the closed economy, it requires that aggregate expenditure E\mathcal{E}E equals aggregate output YYY:

Y=C(Y−T)+I(r)+G.Y = C(Y - T) + I(r) + G.Y=C(Y−T)+I(r)+G.
(1)

Using a linear consumption function C(yd)=a+bYdC(y^d) = a + bY^dC(yd)=a+bYd with marginal propensity to consume b∈(0,1)b \in (0,1)b∈(0,1) and autonomous consumption a>0a > 0a>0, and the linear investment function I(r)=Iˉ−brrI(r) = \bar{I} - b_r rI(r)=Iˉ−br​r with sensitivity br>0b_r > 0br​>0:

Y=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ−brr+G.Y = a + b(Y - T) + \bar{I} - b_r r + G.Y=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ−br​r+G.
(2)

Rearranging, and using r≈i−πer \approx i - \pi^er≈i−πe with πe\pi^eπe exogenous (so that rrr and iii differ by the constant πe\pi^eπe which we absorb into parameters):

Y−bY=a−bT+Iˉ−bri+G  ⟹  Y(1−b)=Aˉ−bri,Y - bY = a - bT + \bar{I} - b_r i + G \implies Y(1-b) = \bar{A} - b_r i,Y−bY=a−bT+Iˉ−br​i+G⟹Y(1−b)=Aˉ−br​i,
(3)

where Aˉ=a−bT+Iˉ+G+brπe\bar{A} = a - bT + \bar{I} + G + b_r\pi^eAˉ=a−bT+Iˉ+G+br​πe collects all autonomous expenditure. The IS equation is thus:

Y+br1−bi=Aˉ1−b,or equivalentlyY=Aˉ1−b−br1−bi.Y + \frac{b_r}{1-b}i = \frac{\bar{A}}{1-b}, \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad Y = \frac{\bar{A}}{1-b} - \frac{b_r}{1-b}i.Y+1−bbr​​i=1−bAˉ​,or equivalentlyY=1−bAˉ​−1−bbr​​i.
(4)

Writing more compactly with κG≡1/(1−b)\kappa_G \equiv 1/(1-b)κG​≡1/(1−b) (the Keynesian multiplier) and letting βr≡br/(1−b)\beta_r \equiv b_r/(1-b)βr​≡br​/(1−b):

Y=κGAˉ−βri.\boxed{Y = \kappa_G\bar{A} - \beta_r i.}Y=κG​Aˉ−βr​i.​
(5)

This is the IS equation: a downward-sloping relationship in (Y,i)(Y, i)(Y,i) space with slope −1/βr-1/\beta_r−1/βr​ (or equivalently, when plotted with iii on the vertical axis, slope −1/βr-1/\beta_r−1/βr​ in iii per unit of YYY).

6.1.2 The LM Equation¶

The LM curve is the money-market equilibrium condition. Real money demand L(Y,i)=kY−hiL(Y, i) = kY - hiL(Y,i)=kY−hi (where k>0k > 0k>0 is income elasticity and h>0h > 0h>0 is interest semi-elasticity) equals real money supply M/PM/PM/P:

kY−hi=MP.kY - hi = \frac{M}{P}.kY−hi=PM​.
(6)

Solving for iii:

i=khY−1hMP.\boxed{i = \frac{k}{h}Y - \frac{1}{h}\frac{M}{P}.}i=hk​Y−h1​PM​.​
(7)

This is the LM equation: an upward-sloping relationship in (Y,i)(Y, i)(Y,i) space with slope k/hk/hk/h.

6.2 The IS–LM System in Matrix Form¶

Stacking the IS and LM equations in the form Ay=bA\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}Ay=b:

(1βrk−h)⏟A(Yi)⏟y=(κGAˉ−M/P)⏟b.\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \beta_r \\ k & -h \end{pmatrix}}_{A}\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} Y \\ i \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{y}} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \kappa_G\bar{A} \\ -M/P \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}}.A(1k​βr​−h​)​​y(Yi​)​​=b(κG​Aˉ−M/P​)​​.
(8)

Definition 6.1 (IS–LM Coefficient Matrix). The matrix A=(1βrk−h)A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \beta_r \\ k & -h \end{pmatrix}A=(1k​βr​−h​) encodes the structural parameters of the IS–LM model. It is nonsingular (invertible) when det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0det(A)=0.

Computing the determinant:

det⁡(A)=(1)(−h)−(βr)(k)=−h−βrk=−(h+βrk)<0.\det(A) = (1)(-h) - (\beta_r)(k) = -h - \beta_r k = -(h + \beta_r k) < 0.det(A)=(1)(−h)−(βr​)(k)=−h−βr​k=−(h+βr​k)<0.
(9)

Since h>0h > 0h>0, βr>0\beta_r > 0βr​>0, and k>0k > 0k>0, the determinant is strictly negative, so AAA is always invertible and the IS–LM system always has a unique solution. This is the algebraic counterpart to the graphical statement that the IS and LM curves always intersect in exactly one point (given upward-sloping LM and downward-sloping IS).

6.2.1 Direct Matrix Inversion¶

The inverse of the 2×22\times22×2 matrix AAA:

A−1=1det⁡(A)(−h−βr−k1)=1−(h+βrk)(−h−βr−k1).A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(A)}\begin{pmatrix} -h & -\beta_r \\ -k & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{-(h+\beta_r k)}\begin{pmatrix} -h & -\beta_r \\ -k & 1 \end{pmatrix}.A−1=det(A)1​(−h−k​−βr​1​)=−(h+βr​k)1​(−h−k​−βr​1​).
(10)

The solution y∗=A−1b\mathbf{y}^* = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}y∗=A−1b:

(Y∗i∗)=1h+βrk(hβrk−1)(κGAˉ−M/P).\begin{pmatrix} Y^* \\ i^* \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{h + \beta_r k}\begin{pmatrix} h & \beta_r \\ k & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \kappa_G\bar{A} \\ -M/P \end{pmatrix}.(Y∗i∗​)=h+βr​k1​(hk​βr​−1​)(κG​Aˉ−M/P​).
(11)

Working out the products:

Y∗=hκGAˉ+βr(M/P)h+βrk\boxed{Y^* = \frac{h\kappa_G\bar{A} + \beta_r(M/P)}{h + \beta_r k}}Y∗=h+βr​khκG​Aˉ+βr​(M/P)​​
(12)
i∗=kκGAˉ−(M/P)h+βrk\boxed{i^* = \frac{k\kappa_G\bar{A} - (M/P)}{h + \beta_r k}}i∗=h+βr​kkκG​Aˉ−(M/P)​​
(13)

These are the reduced-form equations of the IS–LM model: they express the endogenous variables (Y∗,i∗)(Y^*, i^*)(Y∗,i∗) entirely in terms of exogenous variables (Aˉ,M/P)(\bar{A}, M/P)(Aˉ,M/P) and structural parameters (b,br,k,h)(b, b_r, k, h)(b,br​,k,h).

6.3 Policy Multipliers via Cramer’s Rule¶

Definition 6.2 (Policy Multiplier). The policy multiplier with respect to instrument zzz is the partial derivative ∂Y∗/∂z\partial Y^*/\partial z∂Y∗/∂z (or ∂i∗/∂z\partial i^*/\partial z∂i∗/∂z), holding all other exogenous variables fixed.

We derive every policy multiplier from the reduced-form solution. Note that Aˉ=a−bT+Iˉ+G+brπe\bar{A} = a - bT + \bar{I} + G + b_r\pi^eAˉ=a−bT+Iˉ+G+br​πe, so ∂Aˉ/∂G=1\partial\bar{A}/\partial G = 1∂Aˉ/∂G=1, ∂Aˉ/∂T=−b\partial\bar{A}/\partial T = -b∂Aˉ/∂T=−b, and ∂Aˉ/∂Iˉ=1\partial\bar{A}/\partial\bar{I} = 1∂Aˉ/∂Iˉ=1.

6.3.1 The Fiscal Multiplier¶

μG=∂Y∗∂G=hκGh+βrk=h/(1−b)h+brk/(1−b)=hh(1−b)+brk.\mu_G = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial G} = \frac{h\kappa_G}{h + \beta_r k} = \frac{h/(1-b)}{h + b_r k/(1-b)} = \frac{h}{h(1-b) + b_r k}.μG​=∂G∂Y∗​=h+βr​khκG​​=h+br​k/(1−b)h/(1−b)​=h(1−b)+br​kh​.
(14)

Writing br=brb_r = b_rbr​=br​ (not divided by 1−b1-b1−b) and κG=1/(1−b)\kappa_G = 1/(1-b)κG​=1/(1−b):

μG=hh+brk⋅11−b=hh(1−b)+brk.\boxed{\mu_G = \frac{h}{h + b_r k} \cdot \frac{1}{1-b} = \frac{h}{h(1-b) + b_r k}.}μG​=h+br​kh​⋅1−b1​=h(1−b)+br​kh​.​
(15)

This is always strictly less than κG=1/(1−b)\kappa_G = 1/(1-b)κG​=1/(1−b), the Keynesian cross multiplier. The ratio μG/κG=h(1−b)/(h(1−b)+brk)<1\mu_G/\kappa_G = h(1-b)/(h(1-b)+b_r k) < 1μG​/κG​=h(1−b)/(h(1−b)+br​k)<1 measures how much of the Keynesian cross multiplier survives after accounting for the interest rate feedback — the crowding-out factor.

Definition 6.3 (Crowding Out). The reduction in private investment caused by the rise in the interest rate following a fiscal expansion is called crowding out. In the IS–LM model, a fiscal expansion of ΔG\Delta GΔG raises the interest rate by:

Δi∗=kh+βrk⋅κGΔG=kh(1−b)+brkΔG>0,\Delta i^* = \frac{k}{h + \beta_r k}\cdot\kappa_G\Delta G = \frac{k}{h(1-b) + b_r k}\Delta G > 0,Δi∗=h+βr​kk​⋅κG​ΔG=h(1−b)+br​kk​ΔG>0,
(16)

which reduces investment by brΔi∗>0b_r\Delta i^* > 0br​Δi∗>0. The gross fiscal effect on output (κGΔG\kappa_G\Delta GκG​ΔG) is partially offset by the investment crowding-out (−brΔi∗=−brkκGΔG/(h+βrk)-b_r\Delta i^* = -b_r k\kappa_G\Delta G/(h + \beta_r k)−br​Δi∗=−br​kκG​ΔG/(h+βr​k)):

ΔY∗=κGΔG⏟gross IS shift−brkκGh+βrkΔG⏟crowding out=hh+βrkκGΔG.\Delta Y^* = \underbrace{\kappa_G\Delta G}_{\text{gross IS shift}} - \underbrace{\frac{b_r k\kappa_G}{h + \beta_r k}\Delta G}_{\text{crowding out}} = \frac{h}{h + \beta_r k}\kappa_G\Delta G.ΔY∗=gross IS shiftκG​ΔG​​−crowding outh+βr​kbr​kκG​​ΔG​​=h+βr​kh​κG​ΔG.
(17)

Theorem 6.1 (Crowding-Out Formula). In the IS–LM model, the fraction of the Keynesian cross multiplier that survives crowding out is:

Crowding-out factor=1−brkh+brk=hh+brk.\text{Crowding-out factor} = 1 - \frac{b_r k}{h + b_r k} = \frac{h}{h + b_r k}.Crowding-out factor=1−h+br​kbr​k​=h+br​kh​.
(18)

Proof. Direct substitution of the two multiplier expressions above. □\square□

Two limiting cases:

  1. Liquidity trap: h→∞h \to \inftyh→∞. Then μG→κG\mu_G \to \kappa_GμG​→κG​ — the IS–LM multiplier equals the Keynesian cross multiplier. When money demand is perfectly elastic, the interest rate doesn’t rise in response to fiscal expansion (the LM is horizontal), so there is zero crowding out.

  2. Classical case: h→0h \to 0h→0 (money demand completely interest-inelastic). Then μG→0\mu_G \to 0μG​→0 — fiscal policy is completely ineffective. The LM is vertical; any income increase raises money demand, which drives up the interest rate until investment falls by exactly ΔG\Delta GΔG. Complete crowding out.

μT=∂Y∗∂T=hκG(−b)h+βrk=−bhh(1−b)+brk.\mu_T = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial T} = \frac{h\kappa_G(-b)}{h + \beta_r k} = -\frac{bh}{h(1-b) + b_r k}.μT​=∂T∂Y∗​=h+βr​khκG​(−b)​=−h(1−b)+br​kbh​.
(19)
μT=−bhh(1−b)+brk=−b⋅μG/h⋅h=−b1−b⋅hh+brk/(1−b)\boxed{\mu_T = -\frac{bh}{h(1-b) + b_r k} = -b\cdot\mu_G/h \cdot h = -\frac{b}{1-b}\cdot\frac{h}{h+b_rk/(1-b)}}μT​=−h(1−b)+br​kbh​=−b⋅μG​/h⋅h=−1−bb​⋅h+br​k/(1−b)h​​
(20)

More cleanly: μT=−b/(1−b)⋅(h/(h+brk))⋅(1−b)=−bh/[h(1−b)+brk]\mu_T = -b/(1-b) \cdot (h/(h+b_r k)) \cdot (1-b) = -bh/[h(1-b)+b_rk]μT​=−b/(1−b)⋅(h/(h+br​k))⋅(1−b)=−bh/[h(1−b)+br​k]. Since ∣μT∣=b⋅∣μG/(1−b)∣⋅(1−b)<∣μG∣|\mu_T| = b\cdot|\mu_G/(1-b)| \cdot (1-b) < |\mu_G|∣μT​∣=b⋅∣μG​/(1−b)∣⋅(1−b)<∣μG​∣, we confirm ∣μT∣<μG|\mu_T| < \mu_G∣μT​∣<μG​: tax cuts are less stimulative than equivalent spending increases (each dollar of spending creates a full dollar of first-round demand; each dollar of tax cut is only partially spent).

6.3.3 The Monetary Policy Multiplier¶

A monetary expansion increases the real money supply M/PM/PM/P:

μM=∂Y∗∂(M/P)=βrh+βrk=br/(1−b)h+brk/(1−b).\mu_M = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial(M/P)} = \frac{\beta_r}{h + \beta_r k} = \frac{b_r/(1-b)}{h + b_r k/(1-b)}.μM​=∂(M/P)∂Y∗​=h+βr​kβr​​=h+br​k/(1−b)br​/(1−b)​.
(21)
μM=brh(1−b)+brk.\boxed{\mu_M = \frac{b_r}{h(1-b) + b_r k}.}μM​=h(1−b)+br​kbr​​.​
(22)

Monetary policy works by reducing the interest rate (∂i∗/∂(M/P)=−1/(h+βrk)<0\partial i^*/\partial(M/P) = -1/(h+\beta_rk) < 0∂i∗/∂(M/P)=−1/(h+βr​k)<0), which stimulates investment, which raises income through the multiplier. The monetary multiplier is zero when br=0b_r = 0br​=0 (investment insensitive to interest rates — the IS is vertical) or when h→∞h \to \inftyh→∞ (liquidity trap).

6.4 Comparative Statics via the Implicit Function Theorem¶

The multiplier formulas above were derived from the explicit reduced form. An alternative, more general method uses the IFT [M:Ch.1.5] directly on the equilibrium conditions without first solving for Y∗Y^*Y∗ explicitly.

The equilibrium conditions define an implicit function F(Y,i;G,T,M/P)=0F(Y, i; G, T, M/P) = \mathbf{0}F(Y,i;G,T,M/P)=0 where:

F1=Y−κGAˉ+βri=0(IS)F_1 = Y - \kappa_G\bar{A} + \beta_r i = 0 \quad \text{(IS)}F1​=Y−κG​Aˉ+βr​i=0(IS)
(23)
F2=kY−hi−M/P=0(LM)F_2 = kY - hi - M/P = 0 \quad \text{(LM)}F2​=kY−hi−M/P=0(LM)
(24)

The Jacobian with respect to endogenous variables:

∂F∂(Y,i)=(1βrk−h)=A.\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial(Y,i)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \beta_r \\ k & -h \end{pmatrix} = A.∂(Y,i)∂F​=(1k​βr​−h​)=A.
(25)

By the IFT (Theorem 1.8, multivariate version):

d(Y∗,i∗)dz=−A−1∂F∂z,\frac{d(Y^*, i^*)}{d\mathbf{z}} = -A^{-1}\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial\mathbf{z}},dzd(Y∗,i∗)​=−A−1∂z∂F​,
(26)

where z\mathbf{z}z is any exogenous variable vector. For z=Gz = Gz=G:

∂F∂G=(−κG0).\frac{\partial\mathbf{F}}{\partial G} = \begin{pmatrix} -\kappa_G \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.∂G∂F​=(−κG​0​).
(27)

Therefore:

(∂Y∗/∂G∂i∗/∂G)=−A−1(−κG0)=1h+βrk(hκGkκG),\begin{pmatrix}\partial Y^*/\partial G \\ \partial i^*/\partial G\end{pmatrix} = -A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}-\kappa_G \\ 0\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{h+\beta_r k}\begin{pmatrix}h\kappa_G \\ k\kappa_G\end{pmatrix},(∂Y∗/∂G∂i∗/∂G​)=−A−1(−κG​0​)=h+βr​k1​(hκG​kκG​​),
(28)

recovering μG=hκG/(h+βrk)\mu_G = h\kappa_G/(h+\beta_r k)μG​=hκG​/(h+βr​k) and ∂i∗/∂G=kκG/(h+βrk)>0\partial i^*/\partial G = k\kappa_G/(h+\beta_r k) > 0∂i∗/∂G=kκG​/(h+βr​k)>0. The IFT method is particularly convenient when the system has many variables and one does not want to invert the full matrix algebraically.

6.5 The Mundell–Fleming Model: A 3×3 System¶

The open economy adds the foreign exchange market (BP curve) to the IS–LM system, yielding a 3×3 linear system determining (Y∗,i∗,e∗)(Y^*, i^*, e^*)(Y∗,i∗,e∗) where eee is the exchange rate (or the current-account balance, depending on the exchange rate regime).

6.5.1 The Three Equations¶

IS (open economy): Aggregate demand includes net exports NX(Y,Y∗,e)=X(Y∗,e)−Mimports(Y,e)NX(Y, Y^*, e) = X(Y^*, e) - M^{imports}(Y, e)NX(Y,Y∗,e)=X(Y∗,e)−Mimports(Y,e):

Y=κopenAˉopen−βri+βee,Y = \kappa^{open}\bar{A}^{open} - \beta_r i + \beta_e e,Y=κopenAˉopen−βr​i+βe​e,
(29)

where κopen=1/(1−b+mY)\kappa^{open} = 1/(1-b+m_Y)κopen=1/(1−b+mY​) (with mYm_YmY​ the marginal propensity to import) and βe>0\beta_e > 0βe​>0 captures the expenditure-switching effect: a higher eee (weaker domestic currency) improves net exports.

LM (same as closed):

kY−hi=M/P.kY - hi = M/P.kY−hi=M/P.
(30)

BP (balance of payments): For the capital account KA=κi(i−i∗)KA = \kappa_i(i - i^*)KA=κi​(i−i∗) where i∗i^*i∗ is the world interest rate, and trade balance TB=TB0+θee−mYYTB = TB_0 + \theta_e e - m_Y YTB=TB0​+θe​e−mY​Y, the BP equilibrium TB+KA=0TB + KA = 0TB+KA=0:

−mYY+θee+κi(i−i∗)=0  ⟹  −mYY+κii+θee=κii∗.-m_Y Y + \theta_e e + \kappa_i(i - i^*) = 0 \implies -m_Y Y + \kappa_i i + \theta_e e = \kappa_i i^*.−mY​Y+θe​e+κi​(i−i∗)=0⟹−mY​Y+κi​i+θe​e=κi​i∗.
(31)

The 3×3 system Ay=bA\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}Ay=b with y=(Y,i,e)′\mathbf{y} = (Y, i, e)'y=(Y,i,e)′:

(1βr−βek−h0−mYκiθe)⏟A(Yie)=(κopenAˉopenM/Pκii∗)⏟b.\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \beta_r & -\beta_e \\ k & -h & 0 \\ -m_Y & \kappa_i & \theta_e \end{pmatrix}}_{A}\begin{pmatrix} Y \\ i \\ e \end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \kappa^{open}\bar{A}^{open} \\ M/P \\ \kappa_i i^* \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}}.A⎝⎛​1k−mY​​βr​−hκi​​−βe​0θe​​⎠⎞​​​⎝⎛​Yie​⎠⎞​=b⎝⎛​κopenAˉopenM/Pκi​i∗​⎠⎞​​​.
(32)

The solution y∗=A−1b\mathbf{y}^* = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}y∗=A−1b requires inverting this 3×33\times33×3 matrix — straightforward with APL’s ⌹ but algebraically complex by hand.

6.5.2 Exchange Rate Regimes and the Trilemma¶

The Mundell–Fleming model takes its most elegant form under the two polar exchange rate regimes, because each regime eliminates one endogenous variable.

Fixed exchange rate (e=eˉe = \bar{e}e=eˉ fixed, M/PM/PM/P endogenous): The exchange rate is no longer a variable; the BP equation pins down the money supply required to maintain eˉ\bar{e}eˉ. The system reduces to a 2×22\times22×2 problem in (Y,i)(Y, i)(Y,i) with e=eˉe = \bar{e}e=eˉ substituted. The fiscal multiplier under fixed rates with perfect capital mobility (κi→∞\kappa_i \to\inftyκi​→∞):

μGfixed, perfect=κopen=11−b+mY.\mu_G^{fixed,\, perfect} = \kappa^{open} = \frac{1}{1-b+m_Y}.μGfixed,perfect​=κopen=1−b+mY​1​.
(33)

There is no crowding out under a fixed exchange rate with perfect capital mobility! The BP curve forces i=i∗i = i^*i=i∗; any tendency for the domestic interest rate to rise above i∗i^*i∗ immediately attracts capital inflows, expanding the money supply and keeping i=i∗i = i^*i=i∗. The fiscal expansion faces no interest-rate headwind.

Flexible exchange rate (eee endogenous, M/PM/PM/P fixed): Under perfect capital mobility, the capital inflows triggered by a fiscal expansion appreciate the exchange rate (eee falls, domestic currency strengthens), crowding out net exports until ΔY∗=0\Delta Y^* = 0ΔY∗=0. Fiscal policy is completely ineffective. But monetary policy — which works through the exchange rate — is fully potent.

Theorem 6.2 (Mundell–Fleming Trilemma, Algebraic Form). Under perfect capital mobility (κi→∞\kappa_i \to\inftyκi​→∞), the fiscal multiplier satisfies:

μGfixed=κopen>0,μGflexible=0.\mu_G^{fixed} = \kappa^{open} > 0, \quad \mu_G^{flexible} = 0.μGfixed​=κopen>0,μGflexible​=0.
(34)

Proof sketch. Under perfect capital mobility, i=i∗i = i^*i=i∗ at all times. Under a fixed exchange rate, this constraint is satisfied by adjusting MMM, so the LM curve accommodates the fiscal expansion. Under a flexible exchange rate, MMM is fixed, so the LM curve cannot shift — the only way to maintain i=i∗i = i^*i=i∗ is through exchange rate appreciation which eliminates the net-export stimulus exactly. □\square□

6.6 Worked Example: Full Solution Under Fixed and Flexible Rates¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 21 (exchange rates, UIP, trilemma) [P:Ch.21]

Calibration:

  • b=0.75b = 0.75b=0.75 (MPC), mY=0.15m_Y = 0.15mY​=0.15 (marginal propensity to import), br=2b_r = 2br​=2 (investment-interest sensitivity)

  • h=4h = 4h=4 (interest semi-elasticity of money demand), k=0.5k = 0.5k=0.5 (income elasticity of money demand)

  • βe=1.5\beta_e = 1.5βe​=1.5 (exchange rate effect on net exports), θe=0.8\theta_e = 0.8θe​=0.8, κi=10\kappa_i = 10κi​=10 (capital mobility)

  • Aˉopen=400\bar{A}^{open} = 400Aˉopen=400, M/P=500M/P = 500M/P=500, i∗=0.04i^* = 0.04i∗=0.04

IS–LM solution (closed economy, for reference):

κG=1/(1−0.75)=4\kappa_G = 1/(1-0.75) = 4κG​=1/(1−0.75)=4, βr=2/0.25=8\beta_r = 2/0.25 = 8βr​=2/0.25=8

Y∗=(4×400×h+8×500)/(h+8×0.5)=(6400+4000)/8=10400/8=1300Y^* = (4 \times 400 \times h + 8 \times 500)/(h + 8 \times 0.5) = (6400 + 4000)/8 = 10400/8 = 1300Y∗=(4×400×h+8×500)/(h+8×0.5)=(6400+4000)/8=10400/8=1300

i∗=(0.5×4×400−500)/(4+8×0.5)=(800−500)/8=37.5i^* = (0.5 \times 4 \times 400 - 500)/(4 + 8 \times 0.5) = (800 - 500)/8 = 37.5i∗=(0.5×4×400−500)/(4+8×0.5)=(800−500)/8=37.5

(Note: i∗i^*i∗ in these units is not a realistic interest rate — the calibration is illustrative.)

Fiscal multipliers:

μGclosed=h/(h(1−b)+brk)=4/(4×0.25+2×0.5)=4/(1+1)=2.0\mu_G^{closed} = h/(h(1-b)+b_r k) = 4/(4\times0.25 + 2\times0.5) = 4/(1+1) = 2.0μGclosed​=h/(h(1−b)+br​k)=4/(4×0.25+2×0.5)=4/(1+1)=2.0

μGopen, fixed≈κopen=1/(1−0.75+0.15)=1/0.40=2.5\mu_G^{open,\,fixed} \approx \kappa^{open} = 1/(1-0.75+0.15) = 1/0.40 = 2.5μGopen,fixed​≈κopen=1/(1−0.75+0.15)=1/0.40=2.5

μGopen, flexible≈0\mu_G^{open,\,flexible} \approx 0μGopen,flexible​≈0 (complete crowding out via exchange rate appreciation)

Interpretation: Moving from a closed economy to a fixed-exchange-rate open economy raises the fiscal multiplier from 2.0 to 2.5, because the fixed rate prevents the interest rate from rising (capital inflows finance the deficit), eliminating crowding out. Under flexible rates, the multiplier collapses to zero — consistent with Principles Ch. 21 [P:Ch.21.4].

⎕IO←0 ⋄ ⎕ML←1

⍝ 1. Parameters
b ← 0.75  ⋄ b_r ← 2   ⋄ k ← 0.5  ⋄ h ← 4
Abar ← 400 ⋄ MP ← 500 

kg ← ÷ 1 - b                 ⍝ Keynesian multiplier (4.0)
beta_r ← b_r × kg            ⍝ IS slope coefficient (8.0)

⍝ 2. Solve Equilibrium [Y*, i*]
⍝ IS: Y + beta_r*i = kg*Abar
⍝ LM: k*Y - h*i = MP
A ← 2 2 ⍴ 1 beta_r k (-h)
b_vec ← (kg × Abar) MP
eq ← b_vec ⌹ A

'Equilibrium [Y, i]:' (4 ⍕ eq)

⍝ 3. Multipliers (Fixed Precedence)
⍝ Formula: h / (h(1-b) + b_r*k)
⍝ We write it R-to-L friendly: h ÷ (b_r×k) + h×1-b
denom ← (b_r × k) + h × 1 - b
mu_G ← h ÷ denom
mu_T ← (¯1 × b × h) ÷ denom
mu_M ← b_r ÷ denom

'Multipliers [G, T, M]:' (4 ⍕ mu_G mu_T mu_M)

⍝ 4. Sensitivity Grid (Fixed ∞ and Precedence)
H ← 0.5 1 2 4 8 1e6          ⍝ Use 1e6 for "Infinity"
BR ← 0.5 1 2 4
⍝ Logic: ⍺ is h, ⍵ is b_r
grid ← H ∘.{⍺ ÷ (⍵ × k) + ⍺ × 1 - b} BR

'Spending Multiplier Grid (Rows=h, Cols=br):'
⍪ ⍕ 2 ⍕ grid

# Python — IS-LM system: solve and compute all multipliers
import numpy as np
from sympy import symbols, Matrix, simplify, latex

# Numeric solution
b, b_r, k, h = 0.75, 2.0, 0.5, 4.0
kg = 1/(1-b); beta_r = b_r*kg
Abar, MP = 400, 500

A = np.array([[1, beta_r], [k, -h]])
rhs = np.array([kg*Abar, -MP])
Y_star, i_star = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)
print(f"Y* = {Y_star:.2f},  i* = {i_star:.4f}")

denom = h*(1-b) + b_r*k
mu_G = h/denom; mu_T = -b*h/denom; mu_M = b_r/denom
print(f"μ_G = {mu_G:.3f},  μ_T = {mu_T:.3f},  μ_M = {mu_M:.3f}")

# Symbolic multipliers via sympy
b_s, br_s, k_s, h_s = symbols('b b_r k h', positive=True)
denom_s = h_s*(1-b_s) + br_s*k_s
print("Symbolic μ_G =", simplify(h_s/denom_s))
# Julia — IS-LM with parameter sweep
b, b_r, k, h = 0.75, 2.0, 0.5, 4.0
kg = 1/(1-b); beta_r = b_r*kg

A = [1 beta_r; k -h]
rhs = [kg*400.0, -500.0]
Y_star, i_star = A \ rhs
println("Y* = $(round(Y_star,digits=2)), i* = $(round(i_star,digits=4))")

# Sensitivity: multiplier grid over h and b_r
h_vals = [0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 100]
br_vals = [0.5, 1, 2, 4]
println("\nFiscal multiplier grid (rows=h, cols=b_r):")
grid = [h_v / (h_v*(1-b) + br_v*k) for h_v in h_vals, br_v in br_vals]
display(round.(grid, digits=3))
# R — IS-LM with symbolic Cramer's rule via Ryacas
library(Ryacas)

# Define symbolic variables
b_s <- ysym("b"); br_s <- ysym("b_r"); k_s <- ysym("k"); h_s <- ysym("h")
Ag_s <- ysym("A_bar"); MP_s <- ysym("M_P")

# IS-LM matrix (symbolic)
A_sym <- ysym("{{1, b_r/(1-b)}, {k, -h}}")
b_sym <- ysym("{A_bar/(1-b), -M_P}")
sol   <- yac_str(paste0("Inverse(", as.character(A_sym), ") . ", as.character(b_sym)))
cat("Symbolic solution:\n", sol, "\n")

# Numeric
b <- 0.75; b_r <- 2; k <- 0.5; h <- 4
A_num <- matrix(c(1, k, b_r/(1-b), -h), 2, 2)
b_num <- c(400/(1-b), -500)
solution <- solve(A_num, b_num)
cat(sprintf("Y* = %.2f, i* = %.4f\n", solution[1], solution[2]))

6.8 Chapter Summary¶

Key results:

  • The IS–LM model is a 2×22\times22×2 linear system Ay=bA\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}Ay=b with coefficient matrix A=(1βrk−h)A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & \beta_r \\ k & -h\end{pmatrix}A=(1k​βr​−h​) and det⁡(A)=−(h+βrk)<0\det(A) = -(h+\beta_r k) < 0det(A)=−(h+βr​k)<0, guaranteeing a unique solution.

  • The fiscal multiplier μG=h/[h(1−b)+brk]\mu_G = h/[h(1-b)+b_r k]μG​=h/[h(1−b)+br​k] lies between 0 (classical LM) and κG=1/(1−b)\kappa_G = 1/(1-b)κG​=1/(1−b) (liquidity trap), with crowding out being the source of the gap.

  • The tax multiplier μT=−bh/[h(1−b)+brk]=bμT\mu_T = -bh/[h(1-b)+b_r k] = b\mu_TμT​=−bh/[h(1−b)+br​k]=bμT​ is smaller in absolute value than μG\mu_GμG​: tax cuts are less potent than spending increases.

  • The monetary multiplier μM=br/[h(1−b)+brk]\mu_M = b_r/[h(1-b)+b_r k]μM​=br​/[h(1−b)+br​k] vanishes in the liquidity trap (h→∞h\to\inftyh→∞) and when investment is interest-insensitive (br→0b_r \to 0br​→0).

  • In the Mundell–Fleming model: under fixed exchange rates with perfect capital mobility, μG→κopen\mu_G \to \kappa^{open}μG​→κopen (no crowding out); under flexible rates, μG→0\mu_G \to 0μG​→0 (complete crowding out via exchange rate appreciation).

  • In APL: the entire IS–LM solution is b_vec ⌹ A; the multiplier grid is generated via ∘.f outer product in a single expression.

Connections forward: Chapter 7 derives the Keynesian cross multiplier as the h→∞h\to\inftyh→∞ limit of the IS–LM fiscal multiplier. Chapter 8 embeds IS–LM inside the AD–AS framework, adding price level determination. Chapter 9 derives the ELB multiplier — the h→∞h\to\inftyh→∞ analogue for the dynamic NK model.
